title: Transaction Isolation Levels
tagline: Dirty reads, phantom rows, and the spectrum of isolation that keeps concurrent transactions from stepping on each other.

sections.content:
When hundreds of transactions run concurrently, they can interfere in subtle ways. One transaction might read a row that another hasn't committed yet — a **dirty read**. A repeated query inside the same transaction might return different rows — a **non-repeatable read**. A range query might suddenly see new rows inserted by another transaction — a **phantom read**.

SQL defines four **isolation levels** — Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable — each trading concurrency for correctness. Modern databases like PostgreSQL implement these using **Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)**, which lets readers and writers proceed simultaneously without blocking each other by maintaining multiple row versions.

  T1->>DB: "UPDATE balance = 500 (uncommitted)"
  T2->>DB: "SELECT balance"

  T1->>DB: "ROLLBACK"
  Note over T2: "T2 read data that never existed"
sections.caption: Dirty read: T2 sees T1's uncommitted change. If T1 rolls back, T2 has operated on phantom data.

sections.title: The Whiteboard in the Meeting Room
sections.content: Imagine two colleagues sharing a whiteboard. Under Read Uncommitted, you can read your colleague's half-finished scribbles before they're done — dangerous if they erase it all. Read Committed lets you only read what's been confirmed written with a marker. Repeatable Read means you take a photo of the board at the start; you always see that snapshot even if someone erases and rewrites. Serializable locks the room door — only one person writes at a time, perfectly consistent but slower.

**Read Uncommitted** is the weakest level. A transaction can see uncommitted changes from others. This allows dirty reads and is almost never used in production because it can expose data that may be rolled back.

**Read Committed** is the default in PostgreSQL and most RDBMS. Each statement sees only rows committed before *that statement* began. Dirty reads are prevented, but **non-repeatable reads** are possible — two identical SELECTs in the same transaction may return different values if another transaction committed between them.

**Repeatable Read** takes a snapshot at the start of the transaction. Every SELECT in the transaction sees the same version of committed data from that point. This prevents non-repeatable reads. PostgreSQL's implementation also prevents **phantom reads** (unlike the SQL standard, which only requires Serializable to prevent them).

**Serializable** is the strictest level. Transactions execute as if they ran one after the other, even when concurrent. It catches anomalies that MVCC snapshots miss — for example, two transactions reading the same rows then each deciding to insert based on what they saw. PostgreSQL implements this with **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, tracking read/write dependencies and aborting cycles.

**MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)** is the engine behind most modern isolation. Instead of locking rows during reads, the database keeps old row versions in an undo log or version chain. A reader gets a consistent snapshot without blocking writers; a writer creates a new row version without blocking readers. Postgres's `xmin`/`xmax` transaction IDs on each row tuple implement this. Dead row versions are cleaned up by the **autovacuum** process.

sections.caption: Each level adds a guarantee at the cost of some concurrency. Most systems default to Read Committed.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Repeatable Read locks your snapshot so repeated reads return identical results. Serializable goes further — if another transaction's writes would change what you read, Postgres aborts your transaction with a serialization error that you must retry. Always handle `ERROR 40001` (serialization_failure) with retry logic.

sections.label: Concept
sections.code:
-- Anomaly reference table
-- Isolation Level     | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable | Phantom
-- ------------------  | ---------- | -------------- | -------
-- Read Uncommitted    |  Possible  |   Possible     | Possible
-- Read Committed      | Prevented  |   Possible     | Possible
-- Repeatable Read     | Prevented  |  Prevented     | Possible*
-- Serializable        | Prevented  |  Prevented     | Prevented
-- (* PostgreSQL Repeatable Read also prevents phantoms in practice)

-- MVCC visibility rule (simplified)
-- A row version is visible to transaction T if:
--   xmin (creator tx) is committed AND xmin < T.snapshot_xid
--   AND (xmax (deleter tx) is NOT committed OR xmax > T.snapshot_xid)

-- Check current isolation level
SHOW transaction_isolation;

-- Set default isolation level for a session
SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

sections.content: Most applications work correctly with **Read Committed** (the default). Upgrade to **Repeatable Read** when a transaction reads data multiple times and decisions depend on consistency across those reads — for example, generating a financial report. Use **Serializable** only when correctness is critical and you have retry logic for serialization failures. Avoid Read Uncommitted entirely.

items: **Dirty reads** occur when a transaction sees uncommitted changes; prevented by Read Committed and higher.
**Non-repeatable reads** occur when the same row returns different values in one transaction; prevented by Repeatable Read and higher.
**Phantom reads** occur when a repeated range query returns new rows inserted by another transaction; prevented by Serializable (and in practice by PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read).
**MVCC** avoids read/write locking by keeping multiple row versions — readers get a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.
**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)** detects read/write dependency cycles and aborts transactions to prevent anomalies; design retry logic around `ERROR 40001`.

quiz.question: Which isolation level allows a transaction to read uncommitted changes from another transaction?
quiz.explanation: Read Uncommitted is the weakest level and permits dirty reads — seeing changes that another transaction has not yet committed and may still roll back.

quiz.question: Transaction T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values because T2 committed between the two reads. This anomaly is called:
quiz.explanation: A non-repeatable read happens when the same SELECT within one transaction returns different data for an existing row because another committed transaction modified it between the two reads.

quiz.question: What is a phantom read?
options: Reading a row that was deleted mid-transaction
Seeing a new row in a repeated range query that wasn't there before
Two transactions reading the same row at the same time
A read that returns NULL instead of the actual value
quiz.explanation: Phantom reads occur when a transaction repeats a range query (e.g., WHERE status = 'pending') and sees new rows inserted and committed by another transaction between the two reads.

quiz.question: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explanation: PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed, which prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads. This is also the default for most relational databases.

quiz.question: How does MVCC allow readers and writers to proceed concurrently?
options: It queues all reads behind writes so they see final state
It maintains multiple row versions so readers get a snapshot without blocking writers
It copies the entire table to a read buffer on transaction start
It uses shared locks that readers and writers both acquire
quiz.explanation: MVCC stores multiple versions of each row. Readers access a consistent snapshot based on transaction IDs without acquiring row locks, so they never block writers and vice versa.

quiz.question: A transaction at Serializable isolation level fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. What should the application do?
options: Escalate to a higher isolation level
Report the error to the user and abort
Switch to Read Committed for the retry
quiz.explanation: Serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) are expected with Serializable isolation. The correct response is to retry the transaction from the beginning; the retry will usually succeed.

quiz.question: Which isolation level takes a snapshot at the START of the transaction rather than at each statement?
options: All levels take a per-statement snapshot
quiz.explanation: Repeatable Read captures a snapshot when the transaction begins. All subsequent reads see data as of that moment, preventing non-repeatable reads regardless of concurrent commits.

quiz.question: What PostgreSQL background process cleans up dead MVCC row versions?
quiz.explanation: Autovacuum reclaims space occupied by dead row versions (tuples whose xmax transaction has committed) that are no longer visible to any active transaction.

quiz.question: A financial report transaction reads account balances, computes totals, and inserts them into an audit table. Which isolation level is most appropriate?
options: Read Committed — default is good enough
Repeatable Read — consistent snapshot for all reads
No isolation needed for read-only transactions
quiz.explanation: Repeatable Read ensures all SELECT statements in the transaction see the same snapshot, so aggregates computed across multiple queries are consistent even as other transactions commit.

quiz.question: Under Read Committed, two identical SELECT COUNT(*) queries in the same transaction can return different values. Why?
options: Read Committed allows dirty reads from other transactions
Each statement gets a fresh snapshot, so committed inserts between queries are visible
COUNT(*) bypasses the transaction isolation mechanism
The query planner caches the first result incorrectly
quiz.explanation: Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement, not per transaction. If another transaction inserts and commits rows between your two COUNT queries, the second query will see those rows.
